before.text: Leave hot coffee on the table, and it always cools to room temperature.
It never warms itself back up.
That's entropy at work, and people call entropy disorder.
But what exactly gets messier in a cooling cup?
So what is entropy, really?
Roll two dice: the exact faces, say a three and a four, are a microstate.
The total you read off, seven, is the macrostate.
Of the thirty-six possible face pairs, six total seven, but only one totals two.
So seven comes up six times as often as two.
That's entropy: a count of how many microstates give the same macrostate.
Now swap the dice for gas molecules in a sealed box, an isolated system: no energy or matter gets in or out.
First, the gas crowds into the left half, behind a partition.
Then the partition lifts, and the molecules move randomly, hopping between microstates.
Soon the gas fills the whole box, though nothing pushes it there.
So why does it spread?
Zoom in on a box with just four molecules.
Each molecule can sit in the left half or the right half.
That gives sixteen microstates, and only one has all four on the left.
So what are the chances that a hundred molecules all sit on the left at once?
About one in ten to the thirtieth power.
A real gas has vastly more molecules, so it never gathers back into one half.
Back in the big box, the spread-out macrostate has overwhelmingly more microstates.
That's the second law of thermodynamics: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
It rises until it reaches its maximum, at equilibrium.
A common mistake is to think entropy means disorder.
But entropy counts microstates, not messiness: the spread-out gas has more entropy because it has more ways to be arranged.
Now, why does the coffee cool?
Energy flows from the hot coffee into the cooler room air, spreading among more particles and raising the total microstates.
Each entropy change is the heat transferred divided by the absolute temperature.
The hot coffee loses heat at a high temperature, so its entropy drops a little.
The room air gains that same heat at a lower temperature, so its entropy rises more.
So the total rises, which is why heat never flows from cold to hot on its own.
So entropy counts the ways particles and energy can be arranged.
Things spread out because spread-out arrangements vastly outnumber concentrated ones.
Entropy isn't disorder; it's the number of microstates behind the macrostate you measure.
